```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(phylograftR)
```

<br>
This vignette explains how to **format the inputs** needed to graft missing lineages: the **`missing_taxa_list`** that describes the taxa to graft and the constraints on where they can be grafted, and, optionally, the **`total_richness_per_clades`** that accounts for the species that are neither in the backbone nor in the list (i.e., **unsampled species**).

All the examples use the **toy datasets** shipped with the package: a backbone phylogeny of 30 tips (`toy_backbone`), tables in `.csv` format, and the corresponding R objects.

For a full analysis from scratch, see the main workflow tutorial: `vignette("main_workflow")`.<br>
For the tutorials listed by theme, see: `vignette("phylograftR")`.

<br>

## 1/ What does grafting need?

### The `missing_taxa_list`

Each missing taxon is assigned to a clade of the **backbone phylogeny**, defined by **tips**: a pair of tips whose most recent common ancestor (MRCA) is the clade, or a single tip for a terminal branch.
There are two types of missing lineages, grafted with two functions:

| Type | Grafting function | Clade item | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Missing **taxa** | `graft_missing_taxa()` | `Target_clade` | The taxon is grafted **within** its target clade. |
| Missing **clades** | `graft_missing_clades()` | `Sister_clade` | The taxa sharing the same sister clade are grafted **together**, as one missing clade attached to the stem branch of their sister clade. |

The `missing_taxa_list` is a list with the following items. Every item is **named after the taxa** (`$Taxon_name`):

| Item | Used for | Content |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `Taxon_name` | Both | Names of the taxa to graft. They must be unique and absent from the backbone. |
| `Target_clade` or `Sister_clade` | Taxa / Clades | One clade per taxon (a vector of tips). |
| `Target_clade_name` or `Sister_clade_name` | Both | (Optional) Names of the clades, to make outputs easier to read. |
| `include_target_clade_stem` | Taxa | (Optional) Can the taxon be grafted on the stem branch of its target clade? |
| `Excluded_subclades` | Taxa | (Optional) Subclades of the target clade where the taxon is known **not** to belong. |
| `exclude_subclades_stem` | Taxa | (Optional) Is the stem branch of each excluded subclade also excluded? |
| `allowed_states` | Both | (Optional) States of a stochastic map where the taxon can be grafted. See the tutorials on data types. |

### The backbone phylogeny: `phy`

The toy backbone is shown below with its node IDs in blue boxes. We will use them in the following sections.

```{r plot_backbone, fig.height = 6.5, out.width = "100%"}
data(toy_backbone)

# Plot the backbone with the node IDs in label boxes
ape::plot.phylo(toy_backbone, cex = 0.7, no.margin = TRUE, tip.color = "green3")
ape::nodelabels(cex = 0.7, frame = "rect", bg = "lightblue", col = "darkblue")
```

### The `total_richness_per_clades`

Optionally, the grafting functions also use a **`total_richness_per_clades`**: the total number of species of some clades, which accounts for the species that are neither in the backbone nor in the `missing_taxa_list` (unsampled species) when fitting the birth-death models used to draw divergence times. It is built from a table of clades and their total richness, see section 9.


## 2/ Which way to build the list?

The `missing_taxa_list` can be obtained in three ways all returning the **same kind of object**, validated against the backbone. Whatever the way chosen, the list can then be **edited by hand** afterward for finer level of control.

| You have... | Use | Section |
|:---|:---|:---|
| A **taxonomy** of the backbone tips, and the taxonomic groups of the missing taxa | `build_missing_taxa_list_from_taxonomy()` | 3 |
| A table that defines the **clades** directly (with pairs of tips or node IDs) | `build_missing_taxa_list()` for a data.frame already in R, or `import_missing_taxa_list()` for an external file | 4 |
| A list written by hand in R, with **node IDs** defining the clades of interest | `convert_nodes_to_tips()` | 5 |
| **Any of the above**: a list already built that you want to fine-tune further (stem branches, excluded subclades, taxa to keep...) | Edit the list **manually** in R. This is available **independently of the way the list was built** (taxonomy, table/data.frame, or by hand) | 8 |

The taxonomy is the most convenient way to start, as it only requires the **names** of the groups. Defining the clades from a data.frame or an external table offers more **fine-tuning**, as any node of the backbone can be used.

<br>

## 3/ Use a taxonomy: `build_missing_taxa_list_from_taxonomy()`

When the missing taxa are known by their **taxonomic groups** (families, genera, tribes...), they can be used to retrieve the defining tips of the clades of interest (i.e., target clades, excluded subclades, sister clades) directly from the **taxonomy of the backbone tips**.
Two tables are needed, and they can be imported from external files (text or Excel) with `import_taxonomic_table()`:

- the **backbone table**: one row per tip of the backbone, one column per taxonomic level (`type = "backbone"`).
- the **missing taxa table**: one row per taxon to graft, with its taxonomic groups, and the constraints written with group names (`type = "missing_taxa"`).

```{r taxonomy_look}
# ------ Step 1: Look at the taxonomic tables ------ #

# Taxonomy of the backbone: the first column holds the tip labels (`Taxa`)
data(toy_backbone_taxonomic_table)
head(toy_backbone_taxonomic_table)

# Description of the taxa to graft: one row per taxon
data(toy_missing_taxa_taxonomic_table)
toy_missing_taxa_taxonomic_table
```

In the table of missing taxa:

- `Type` states whether the taxon is grafted within a target clade (`"taxa"`), or as part of a missing clade (`"clades"`). 
- `Target_clade` and `Sister_clade` are written with **group names** (e.g., `"Family_B"`), or with the **name of a taxonomic level** (e.g., `"Family"`, meaning the family of the taxon, as written in the column `Family`).
- `Excluded_subclades` are written the same way, several groups being separated by semicolons.

The tables can be imported from external files with the same checks against the backbone:

```{r taxonomy_import}
# ------ Step 2: Import the tables from external files (optional) ------ #

backbone_path <- system.file("extdata", "toy_backbone_taxonomic_table.csv", package = "phylograftR")
missing_taxa_path <- system.file("extdata", "toy_missing_taxa_taxonomic_table.csv",
                                 package = "phylograftR")

# Import the taxonomy of the backbone, checked against the tips of the phylogeny
backbone_taxonomic_table <- import_taxonomic_table(file = backbone_path, type = "backbone",
                                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE)

# Import the description of the taxa to graft
missing_taxa_taxonomic_table <- import_taxonomic_table(file = missing_taxa_path, type = "missing_taxa",
                                                       phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r taxonomy_build}
# ------ Step 3: Build the missing_taxa_list ------ #

# Taxonomic names are converted into clades of the backbone phylogeny
missing_taxa_lists <- build_missing_taxa_list_from_taxonomy(
  backbone_taxonomic_table = toy_backbone_taxonomic_table,
  missing_taxa_taxonomic_table = toy_missing_taxa_taxonomic_table,
  phy = toy_backbone,
  verbose = FALSE)

# Since both types of taxa were provided, the output has one list per grafting function
names(missing_taxa_lists)
str(missing_taxa_lists$taxa, max.level = 1)

# Clades are written as pairs of tips, and named after their taxonomic groups
missing_taxa_lists$taxa$Target_clade$Genus_a_sp1
missing_taxa_lists$taxa$Target_clade_name

# Taxa to graft as a clade have the same sister clade: they will be grafted together
missing_taxa_lists$clades$Sister_clade_name

# Information on the groups used (clade node, number of tips, monophyly...) can be inspected
# in the attribute "taxonomic_groups"
attr(missing_taxa_lists, "taxonomic_groups")[, c("Group", "Level", "clade_node",
                                                 "n_tips_clade", "monophyletic")]
```

**Non-monophyletic groups.** A taxonomic group is not always monophyletic in the backbone. 
The argument `non_monophyletic` controls what is done:

- `"exclude"` (default) excludes the group from the grafting constraints of the taxa that use it;
- `"mrca"` uses the clade of the MRCA of its tips (which includes tips of other groups);
- `"error"` stops.

The groups, their MRCA node and their monophyly are reported in the attribute `"taxonomic_groups"`, so you can check them.

The groups can only be those of the taxonomy. To use **any clade of the backbone** as a target, sister or excluded clade, define the clades directly with a data.frame (section 4), or edit the list afterwards (section 8).

<br>

## 4/ Build from a data.frame: `build_missing_taxa_list()`

Taxonomic groups are convenient, but they have limits: a clade that is not an identified taxonomic group cannot be used.
`build_missing_taxa_list()` **converts a data.frame** into a `missing_taxa_list`, and gives you **full control** over the constraints: **clades are defined directly on the backbone**, from:

- **tips**: a pair of tips whose MRCA is the clade (`"t26, t18"`), or a single tip;
- **node IDs**: the ID of the node of the backbone, as shown by `ape::nodelabels()` (e.g., `"34"`).

**Any node of the backbone can therefore be a target, sister, or excluded clade**, whatever the taxonomy. This option makes it much easier to **fine-tune** the grafting constraints, for instance to graft a taxon within a clade that is not named in any taxonomy, or to exclude a precise subclade.
Tips and node IDs can be **mixed** between clades, but a single clade is defined by either tips or one node ID.

The data.frame has **one row per taxon**, and each column fills an item of the list:

- `Taxon_name`: name of the taxon to graft.
- `Target_clade` (or `Sister_clade`): tips used to retrieve the MRCA of the clade, separated by commas (`"t26,t18"`), or a node ID (`"34"`).
- `Target_clade_name`: (optional) name of the clade, used in printed reports (`"Genus_1"`).
- `include_target_clade_stem`: `TRUE` or `FALSE`. A blank cell means the default value of the grafting function.
- `Excluded_subclades`: tips (or node IDs) of the subclades. Several subclades are separated by **semicolons**, and the tips of one subclade by **commas** (`"t10,t19;t26,t4"`).
- `Excluded_subclades_names`: names of the subclades, separated by semicolons (`"Tribe_A;Genus_3"`).
- `exclude_subclades_stem`: `TRUE` or `FALSE` with one value per excluded subclade, separated by semicolons (`"TRUE;FALSE"`).

```{r build_df}
# ------ Step 1: Build the missing_taxa_list from a data.frame ------ #

# Write the table in R, with a mix of tips and node IDs (see the plot of the backbone)
my_table <- data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2", "M3"),
                       Target_clade = c("34", "t5, t12", "t26, t18"),
                       Excluded_subclades = c("50", NA, "t10, t19; t26, t4"),
                       Excluded_subclades_names = c(NA, NA, "group_1; group_2"),
                       include_target_clade_stem = c(TRUE, FALSE, NA))
my_table

# The table is checked against the backbone phylogeny.
# Node IDs are converted into tips, and the conversions are printed
my_missing_taxa_list <- build_missing_taxa_list(data = my_table, phy = toy_backbone)
str(my_missing_taxa_list, max.level = 1)

# Node 34 is now defined by a pair of tips whose MRCA is node 34
my_missing_taxa_list$Target_clade$M1
```

Any data.frame can be used, for instance a table loaded in R with `read.csv()`. The function removes extra spaces and treats blank cells and `"NA"` as missing values.

### Import the table from an external file

The table can also be stored in an **external file**, which is convenient to edit it with a spreadsheet, to share it, or to keep it with the data of a project.
`import_missing_taxa_list()` is **equivalent** to reading the file and giving the data.frame to `build_missing_taxa_list()`: it uses the same table format, the same checks and the same conversions of node IDs, and the clades are defined directly on the backbone, with the same flexibility.
Text files (`.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt`) and Excel files (`.xlsx`, `.xls`) are supported, and the format is chosen from the extension of the file.

```{r import_csv}
# ------ Step 2 (optional): Import the table from an external file ------ #

# Path to a table provided with the package
file_path <- system.file("extdata", "toy_missing_taxa.csv", package = "phylograftR")

# One row per taxon, one column per item of the list
read.csv(file_path)

# Import it as a missing_taxa_list, checked against the backbone phylogeny
missing_taxa_list <- import_missing_taxa_list(file = file_path, phy = toy_backbone)

# Items are named after the taxa, tips are split, and excluded subclades are named
str(missing_taxa_list, max.level = 1)

# Example of the clades of one taxon
missing_taxa_list$Target_clade$Genus_a_sp1
missing_taxa_list$Excluded_subclades$Genus_a_sp1
missing_taxa_list$exclude_subclades_stem$Genus_a_sp1

# The result is the same as reading the file and building the list from the data.frame
identical(missing_taxa_list, build_missing_taxa_list(data = read.csv(file_path), phy = toy_backbone))

# The same list is provided as a dataset
data(toy_missing_taxa_list)
identical(missing_taxa_list, toy_missing_taxa_list)
```

To import an **Excel file**, use the same function with the `sheet` argument to select the sheet. It requires the package `readxl`.
Any other format (e.g., `.ods`, or an export of an online spreadsheet) can be read with your own function, provided in `reader`.

```{r import_xlsx, eval = FALSE}
# Import an Excel file
missing_taxa_list <- import_missing_taxa_list(file = "my_missing_taxa.xlsx",
                                              phy = toy_backbone, sheet = "missing_taxa")

# Import any other format with a reader function (e.g., '.ods')
missing_taxa_list <- import_missing_taxa_list(file = "my_missing_taxa.ods", phy = toy_backbone,
                                              reader = readODS::read_ods)
```

<br>

## 5/ Convert node IDs of a list: `convert_nodes_to_tips()`

If you build the **list directly in R**, by hand (without a table), clades can be defined by node IDs too, but the grafting functions only accept **tips**.
`convert_nodes_to_tips()` converts all the node IDs of the list into tips. It also **checks the list against the backbone tree** to make sure that it is valid: items named after `$Taxon_name`, node IDs and tips that exist in the backbone, no mix of tips and node IDs in a clade...
It is used internally by `build_missing_taxa_list()`, `import_missing_taxa_list()` and `build_missing_taxa_list_from_taxonomy()`, so it is only needed for lists written by hand.

```{r convert_nodes}
# A list with clades defined by node IDs, tips, or both
list_with_nodes <- list(
  Taxon_name = c("X1", "X2", "X3"),
  Target_clade = list(X1 = 34, X2 = c("t5", "t12"), X3 = "t26"),
  Excluded_subclades = list(X1 = list(group_1 = 50), X2 = NULL, X3 = NULL))

# Convert the node IDs into tips: the conversions are printed
list_with_tips <- convert_nodes_to_tips(list_with_nodes, phy = toy_backbone)
list_with_tips$Target_clade$X1
```

An internal node is converted into a **pair of tips whose MRCA is the node**, chosen in a deterministic way. 
A clade that is already defined by tips in the list is always defined by the same tips, so the same clade has the same tips in all the objects.
The `total_richness_per_clades` (section 9) can be converted at the same time to keep this consistency: `convert_nodes_to_tips(list, phy, total_richness_per_clades = richness)`.

<br>

## 6/ Species attributes: allowed states

Columns of the table can also restrict the **states of a stochastic map** where each taxon can be grafted. 
For instance, `allowed_states` gives one or several states for each taxon, separated by commas (blank cells mean no restriction for the taxon):

```{r allowed_states}
file_path <- system.file("extdata", "toy_missing_taxa_with_allowed_states.csv", package = "phylograftR")
read.csv(file_path)[, c("Taxon_name", "Target_clade_name", "allowed_states")]

# In this example, the allowed states define color (i.e., "red", "blue", "green") that evolve along the branches of a `simmap`
# and are used to contraint the grafting of each taxon depending on its allowed states.

missing_taxa_list_states <- import_missing_taxa_list(file = file_path, phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE)
missing_taxa_list_states$allowed_states
```

These constraints are used only when a stochastic map (`simmap`) is provided to the grafting function. 
Please refer to the dedicated tutorials explaining how to prepare the maps (`vignette("prepare_trait_data")`) and how to use the ranges and several traits (`vignette("biogeographic_data")` and `vignette("multiple_traits")`) for more detailed information.

<br>

## 7/ Both types of missing lineages in one table

A single table can describe **both types of missing lineages**. With a column `Type` (`"taxa"` or `"clades"`), each row fills the clade item of its type (`Target_clade` or `Sister_clade`). 
Without `Type`, the clade item filled (`Target_clade` or `Sister_clade`) defines the type of the row.
The builders (`import_missing_taxa_list()`, `build_missing_taxa_list()`, `build_missing_taxa_list_from_taxonomy()`) then return a **named list with two elements**, `taxa` and `clades`:

```{r both_types}
# ------ Step 1: A table with both types ------ #

both_table <- data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2", "M3", "M4"),
                         Type = c("taxa", "taxa", "clades", "clades"),
                         Target_clade = c("t26, t18", "t5, t12", NA, NA),
                         Sister_clade = c(NA, NA, "t10, t19", "t10, t19"),
                         Excluded_subclades = c("t26, t4", NA, NA, NA))

# ------ Step 2: Build the lists ------ #

lists <- build_missing_taxa_list(data = both_table, phy = toy_backbone)
names(lists)
lists$taxa$Taxon_name      # Taxa to graft with graft_missing_taxa()
lists$clades$Taxon_name    # Taxa to graft with graft_missing_clades()
lists$clades$Sister_clade  # M3 and M4 have the same sister clade: they form one missing clade
```

This `list(taxa, clades)` is the format expected by `graft_missing_taxa_and_clades()`, which grafts both types in one run, see `vignette("combine_missing_taxa_and_clades")`.
The functions that **check** the grafting before or after (`check_grafting_plan()`, `check_grafting_constraints()`, `extract_grafting_info()`, `extract_sampling_info()`) and `convert_nodes_to_tips()` accept it too. They return a named list with the result of each type, see `vignette("check_grafting")`.
To graft the types separately, use each element with the matching function: `lists$taxa` for `graft_missing_taxa()` and `lists$clades` for `graft_missing_clades()`.

<br>

## 8/ Edit the list manually

The `missing_taxa_list` is a regular R list. Whatever the way it was built (taxonomy, data.frame, external table, or by hand), it can be **edited directly in R** before grafting, and the same edit can also be applied to a list of both types of taxa (section 7), element by element. This is the **final level of fine-tuning** and control: any item can be changed for any taxon.

The rules to keep in mind are:

- every item must remain **named after `$Taxon_name`** and have **one element per taxon** (in the same order);
- clades must be defined by **tips**: if you use node IDs, convert them with `convert_nodes_to_tips()` (see section 5);
- the list of a given type must keep its clade item (`Target_clade` for the missing taxa, `Sister_clade` for the missing clades).

```{r manual_edit}
# ------ Step 1: Edit the list ------ #

# Start from the list of taxa built from the taxonomy (section 3)
taxa_list <- missing_taxa_lists$taxa

# Allow Genus_a_sp3 to be grafted on the stem branch of its target clade
taxa_list$include_target_clade_stem[["Genus_a_sp3"]] <- TRUE

# Add an excluded subclade (and exclude its stem) for Genus_b_sp1
taxa_list$Excluded_subclades[["Genus_b_sp1"]] <- list(Gen_1 = c("t13", "t27"))
taxa_list$exclude_subclades_stem[["Genus_b_sp1"]] <- c(Gen_1 = TRUE)

# Remove a taxon: subset all the items with the same selection
keep <- taxa_list$Taxon_name != "Genus_c_sp2"
taxa_list <- lapply(taxa_list, function (item) item[keep])

# ------ Step 2: Check the edited list ------ #

# The structure of the list and the availability of branches for grafting
# can be checked with check_grafting_plan() (see `vignette("check_grafting")`)
plan <- check_grafting_plan(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = taxa_list, verbose = FALSE)
plan[, c("Taxon_name", "n_branches", "feasible")]
```

The checks stop with an explicit message if the edited list is not valid, for instance if a clade is defined by a node ID, or if an item does not have one element per taxon.

<br>

## 9/ The total richness of clades

The backbone is incomplete, and the missing taxa of the list are not necessarily all the missing species: other species may also be **unsampled** (neither in the backbone nor in the `missing_taxa_list`). 
Their number can be informed with the **total richness** of some clades: the grafting functions then account for them when fitting the birth-death models used to draw divergence times.
Clades without a total richness provided (`NA`) are handled with the information of the clades nested within them: their number of unsampled species is estimated as the sum of unsampled species recorded over the largest clades nested within it (i.e., with a `total_richness` value provided).

A table with the clades and their total richness is converted by `build_total_richness_per_clades()` (internal data.frame) or `import_total_richness_per_clades()` (external file). 
Both need the **`missing_taxa_list`** (or the `list(taxa, clades)`) to check the richness values against the species of the backbone and of the list, and to make sure that the clades are defined by the same tips.

```{r total_richness}
# ------ Step 1: A table with the clades and their total richness ------ #

# Clades are written with their taxonomic names, as in the list built from the taxonomy.
# Use NA if the total richness is unknown
richness_table <- data.frame(Clade = c("Family_A", "Family_B", "Subfam_B1", "Tribe_B2"),
                             total_richness = c(25, NA, 14, 8))

# ------ Step 2: Build the total_richness_per_clades ------ #

# Check against the backbone and the lists of both types
richness_per_clades <- build_total_richness_per_clades(data = richness_table, phy = toy_backbone,
                                                       missing_taxa_list = missing_taxa_lists,
                                                       verbose = FALSE)

# With both types, the output has one element per type. Clades are defined by the same tips as in the lists
names(richness_per_clades)
str(richness_per_clades, max.level = 2)

# ------ Step 3: Check the richness before grafting ------ #

# Expected richness and sampling fraction of each clade
attr(richness_per_clades, "richness_table")[, c("Clade_name", "total_richness", "nb_backbone_species",
                                                "nb_missing_species", "nb_unsampled_species",
                                                "sampling_fraction")]
```

The attribute `"richness_table"` gives the number of species in the backbone, the missing species of the list, and the **unsampled species** deduced from the total richness, and the resulting **sampling fraction** of each clade. 
It can be removed with `return_richness_table = FALSE`.

A table in a file is imported the same way, with the same checks:

```{r total_richness_import}
file_path <- system.file("extdata", "toy_total_richness.csv", package = "phylograftR")
read.csv(file_path)

# The richness table of the toy dataset is defined with tips, and goes with the toy missing_taxa_list
richness <- import_total_richness_per_clades(file = file_path, phy = toy_backbone,
                                             missing_taxa_list = toy_missing_taxa_list,
                                             verbose = FALSE)
str(richness, max.level = 1)
```

The richness is provided to the grafting functions in the argument `total_richness_per_clades`: the list of the matching type to `graft_missing_taxa()` or `graft_missing_clades()`, and the `list(taxa, clades)` to `graft_missing_taxa_and_clades()`.

<br>

## 10/ Common input errors

The functions check the inputs against the backbone and stop with **explicit messages**, before any grafting. Below are the most common cases.

```{r common_errors}
# Helper to display the message of an error
show_error <- function (expr) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(tryCatch(expr, error = function (e) e)), "\n")

# A tip that is not in the backbone (e.g., a typo, or a wrong separator)
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2"), Target_clade = c("t1, t999", "t5")),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))

# Tips and a node ID mixed in the same clade
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2"), Target_clade = c("t1, 34", "t5")),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))

# A node ID that does not exist
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2"), Target_clade = c("t8, t7", "900")),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))

# Duplicated names of taxa
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M1"), Target_clade = c("t8, t7", "t5")),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))

# A taxon to graft that is already a tip of the backbone
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("t5", "M2"), Target_clade = c("t8, t7", "t5")),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))

# A taxon without clade
show_error(build_missing_taxa_list(data.frame(Taxon_name = c("M1", "M2"), Target_clade = c("t8, t7", NA)),
                                   phy = toy_backbone, verbose = FALSE))
```

Node IDs are recognized as text made **only of digits**: tip labels of the backbone must therefore include at least one other character than digits. If some tips are only digits, rename them first.

<br>

## Next steps

With a `missing_taxa_list` (and optionally a `total_richness_per_clades`), you are ready to graft:

- the missing taxa: `graft_missing_taxa()`, see `vignette("graft_taxa")`;
- the missing clades: `graft_missing_clades()`, see `vignette("graft_clades")`;
- both types in one run: `graft_missing_taxa_and_clades()`, see `vignette("combine_missing_taxa_and_clades")`.

The grafting plan can be checked beforehand with `check_grafting_plan()`: `vignette("check_grafting")`.
